172.content: 1 sn Chapter 1 introduces the theme of bondage in Egypt and shows the intensifying opposition to the fulfillment of promises given earlier to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. The first seven verses announce the theme of Israel&apos;s prosperity in Egypt. The second section (vv. 8-14) reports continued prosperity in the face of deliberate opposition. The third section (vv. 15-21) explains the prosperity as divine favor in spite of Pharaoh&apos;s covert attempts at controlling the population. The final verse records a culmination in the developing tyranny and provides a transition to the next section - Pharaoh commands the open murder of the males. The power of God is revealed in the chapter as the people flourish under the forces of evil. However, by the turn of affairs at the end of the chapter, the reader is left with a question about the power of God - &quot;What can God do?&quot; This is good Hebrew narrative, moving the reader through tension after tension to reveal the sovereign power and majesty of the Lord God, but calling for faith every step of the way. See also D. W. Wicke, &quot;The Literary Structure of Exodus 1:2-2:10,&quot; JSOT 24 (1982): 99-107. 2 tn Heb &quot;now these&quot; or &quot;and these.&quot; The vav (ו) disjunctive marks a new beginning in the narrative begun in Genesis. 3 sn The name of the book of Exodus in the Hebrew Bible is שְׁמוֹת (shÿmot), the word for &quot;Names,&quot; drawn from the beginning of the book. The inclusion of the names at this point forms a literary connection to the book of Genesis. It indicates that the Israelites living in bondage had retained a knowledge of their ancestry, and with it, a knowledge of God&apos;s promise. 4 tn The expression בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל (bÿne yisra&apos;el, &quot;sons of Israel&quot;) in most places refers to the nation as a whole and can be translated &quot;Israelites,&quot; although traditionally it has been rendered &quot;the children of Israel&quot; or &quot;the sons of Israel.&quot; Here it refers primarily to the individual sons of the patriarch Israel, for they are named. But the expression is probably also intended to indicate that they are the Israelites (cf. Gen 29:1, &quot;eastern people,&quot; or &quot;easterners,&quot; lit., &quot;sons of the east&quot;). 5 tn Heb &quot;a man and his house.&quot; Since this serves to explain &quot;the sons of Israel,&quot; it has the distributive sense. So while the &quot;sons of Israel&quot; refers to the actual sons of the patriarch, the expression includes their families (cf. NIV, TEV, CEV, NLT).

6 tn The word נֶפֶשׁ (nefesh) is often translated &quot;soul.&quot; But the word refers to the whole person, the body with the soul, and so &quot;life&quot; or &quot;person&quot; is frequently a better translation. 7 tn The expression in apposition to נֶפֶשׁ (nefesh) literally says &quot;those who went out from the loins of Jacob.&quot; This distinguishes the entire company as his direct descendants. 8 sn Gen 46 describes in more detail Jacob&apos;s coming to Egypt with his family. The Greek text of Exod 1:5 and of Gen 46:27 and two Qumran manuscripts, have the number as seventy-five, counting the people a little differently. E. H. Merrill in conjunction with F. Delitzsch notes that the list in Gen 46 of those who entered Egypt includes Hezron and Hamul, who did so in potentia, since they were born after the family entered Egypt. Joseph&apos;s sons are also included, though they too were born in Egypt. &quot;The list must not be pressed too literally&quot; (E. H. Merrill, Kingdom of Priests, 49). 9 tn Heb &quot;and Joseph was in Egypt&quot; (so ASV). The disjunctive word order in Hebrew draws attention to the fact that Joseph, in contrast to his brothers, did not come to Egypt at the same time as Jacob.

10 tn The text simply uses the vav (ו) consecutive with the preterite, &quot;and Joseph died.&quot; While this construction shows sequence with the preceding verse, it does not require that the death follow directly the report of that verse. In fact, readers know from the record in Genesis that the death of Joseph occurred after a good number of years. The statement assumes the passage of time in the natural course of events. 11 tn The verse has a singular verb, &quot;and Joseph died, and all his brothers, and all that generation.&quot; Typical of Hebrew style the verb need only agree with the first of a compound subject. sn Since the deaths of &quot;Joseph and his brothers and all that generation&quot; were common knowledge, their mention must serve some rhetorical purpose. In contrast to the flourishing of Israel, there is death. This theme will appear again: In spite of death in Egypt, the nation flourishes.

12 tn Heb &quot;the sons of Israel.&quot; 13 tn The disjunctive vav marks a contrast with the note about the deaths of the first generation. 14 tn Using מְאֹד (mÿ&apos;od) twice intensifies the idea of their becoming strong (see GKC 431-32 §133.k). sn The text is clearly going out of its way to say that the people of Israel flourished in Egypt. The verbs פָּרָה (parah, &quot;be fruitful&quot;), שָׁרַץ (sharats, &quot;swarm, teem&quot;), רָבָה (ravah, &quot;multiply&quot;), and עָצַם (&apos;atsam, &quot;be strong, mighty&quot;) form a literary link to the creation account in Genesis. The text describes Israel&apos;s prosperity in the terms of God&apos;s original command to be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth, to show that their prosperity was by divine blessing and in compliance with the will of God. The commission for the creation to fill the earth and subdue it would now begin to materialize through the seed of Abraham.

15 sn It would be difficult to identify who this &quot;new king&quot; might be, since the chronology of ancient Israel and Egypt is continually debated. Scholars who take the numbers in the Bible more or less at face value would place the time of Jacob&apos;s going down to Egypt in about 1876 b.c. This would put Joseph&apos;s experience in the period prior to the Hyksos control of Egypt (1720-1570&apos;s), and everything in the narrative about Joseph points to a native Egyptian setting and not a Hyksos one. Joseph&apos;s death, then, would have been around 1806 b.c., just a few years prior to the end of the 12th Dynasty of Egypt. This marked the end of the mighty Middle Kingdom of Egypt. The relationship between the Hyksos (also Semites) and the Israelites may have been amicable, and the Hyksos then might very well be the enemies that the Egyptians feared in Exodus 1:10. It makes good sense to see the new king who did not know Joseph as either the founder (Amosis, 1570-1546) or an early king of the powerful 18th Dynasty (like Thutmose I). Egypt under this new leadership drove out the Hyksos and reestablished Egyptian sovereignty. The new rulers certainly would have been concerned about an increasing Semite population in their territory (see E. H. Merrill, Kingdom of Priests, 49-55). 16 tn The relative clause comes last in the verse in Hebrew. It simply clarifies that the new king had no knowledge about Joseph. It also introduces a major theme in the early portion of Exodus, as a later Pharaoh will claim not to know who Yahweh is. The Lord, however, will work to make sure that Pharaoh and all Egypt will know that he is the true God. 17 tn Heb &quot;arose.&quot;

18 tn Heb &quot;and he said.&quot; 19 tn The particle הִנֵּה (hinneh) introduces the foundational clause for the exhortation to follow by drawing the listeners&apos; attention to the Israelites. In other words, the exhortation that follows is based on this observation. The connection could be rendered &quot;since, because,&quot; or the like.

20 tn The verb is the Hitpael cohortative of חָכַם (khakam, &quot;to be wise&quot;). This verb has the idea of acting shrewdly, dealing wisely. The basic idea in the word group is that of skill. So a skillful decision is required to prevent the Israelites from multiplying any more. sn Pharaoh&apos;s speech invites evaluation. How wise did his plans prove to be? 21 tn The word פֶּן (pen) expresses fear or precaution and can also be translated &quot;lest&quot; or &quot;else&quot; (R. J. Williams, Hebrew Syntax, 75-76, §461). 22 tn The verb can be translated simply &quot;will multiply,&quot; but since Pharaoh has already indicated that he is aware they were doing that, the nuance here must mean to multiply all the more, or to continue to multiply. Cf. NIV &quot;will become even more numerous.&quot; 23 tn The words וְהָיָה כִּי (vÿhayah ki) introduce a conditional clause - &quot;if&quot; (see GKC 335 §112.y). 24 tn Heb &quot;and [lest] he [Israel] also be joined to.&quot; 25 tn Heb &quot;and go up from.&quot; All the verbs coming after the particle פֶּן (pen, &quot;otherwise, lest&quot; in v. 10) have the same force and are therefore parallel. These are the fears of the Egyptians. This explains why a shrewd policy of population control was required. They wanted to keep Israel enslaved; they did not want them to become too numerous and escape.

26 tn Heb &quot;princes of work.&quot; The word שָׂרֵי (sare, &quot;princes&quot;) has been translated using words such as &quot;ruler,&quot; &quot;prince,&quot; &quot;leader,&quot; &quot;official,&quot; &quot;chief,&quot; &quot;commander,&quot; and &quot;captain&quot; in different contexts. It appears again in 2:14 and 18:21 and 25. Hebrew מַס (mas) refers to a labor gang organized to provide unpaid labor, or corvée (Deut 20:11; Josh 17:13; 1 Kgs 9:15, 21). The entire phrase has been translated &quot;foremen,&quot; which combines the idea of oversight and labor. Cf. KJV, NAB, NASB, NRSV &quot;taskmasters&quot;; NIV &quot;slave masters&quot;; NLT &quot;slave drivers.&quot; 27 tn Heb &quot;over them&quot;; the referent (the Israelites) has been specified in the translation for clarity. 28 sn The verb עַנֹּתוֹ (&apos;annoto) is the Piel infinitive construct from עָנָה (&apos;anah, &quot;to oppress&quot;). The word has a wide range of meanings. Here it would include physical abuse, forced subjugation, and humiliation. This king was trying to crush the spirit of Israel by increasing their slave labor. Other terms in the passage that describe this intent include &quot;bitter&quot; and &quot;crushing.&quot; 29 tn The form is a preterite with the vav (ו) consecutive, וַיִּבֶן (vayyiven). The sequence expressed in this context includes the idea of result. 30 sn Many scholars assume that because this city was named Rameses, the Pharaoh had to be Rameses II, and hence that a late date for the exodus (and a late time for the sojourn in Egypt) is proved. But if the details of the context are taken as seriously as the mention of this name, this cannot be the case. If one grants for the sake of discussion that Rameses II was on the throne and oppressing Israel, it is necessary to note that Moses is not born yet. It would take about twenty or more years to build the city, then eighty more years before Moses appears before Pharaoh (Rameses), and then a couple of years for the plagues - this man would have been Pharaoh for over a hundred years. That is clearly not the case for the historical Rameses II. But even more determining is the fact that whoever the Pharaoh was for whom the Israelites built the treasure cities, he died before Moses began the plagues. The Bible says that when Moses grew up and killed the Egyptian, he fled from Pharaoh (whoever that was) and remained in exile until he heard that that Pharaoh had died. So this verse cannot be used for a date of the exodus in the days of Rameses, unless many other details in the chapters are ignored. If it is argued that Rameses was the Pharaoh of the oppression, then his successor would have been the Pharaoh of the exodus. Rameses reigned from 1304 b.c. until 1236 and then was succeeded by Merneptah. That would put the exodus far too late in time, for the Merneptah stela refers to Israel as a settled nation in their land. One would have to say that the name Rameses in this chapter may either refer to an earlier king, or, more likely, reflect an updating in the narrative to name the city according to its later name (it was called something else when they built it, but later Rameses finished it and named it after himself [see B. Jacob, Exodus, 14]). For further discussion see G. L. Archer, &quot;An 18th Dynasty Ramses,&quot; JETS 17 (1974): 49-50; and C. F. Aling, &quot;The Biblical City of Ramses,&quot; JETS 25 (1982): 129-37. Furthermore, for vv. 11-14, see K. A. Kitchen, &quot;From the Brick Fields of Egypt,&quot; TynBul 27 (1976): 137-47.

31 tn Heb &quot;they&quot;; the referent (the Egyptians) has been specified in the translation for clarity. 32 tn The imperfect tenses in this verse are customary uses, expressing continual action in past time (see GKC 315 §107.e). For other examples of כַּאֲשֶׁר (ka&apos;asher) with כֵּן (ken) expressing a comparison (&quot;just as...so&quot;) see Gen 41:13; Judg 1:7; Isa 31:4. sn Nothing in the oppression caused this, of course. Rather, the blessing of God (Gen 12:1-3) was on Israel in spite of the efforts of Egypt to hinder it. According to Gen 15 God had foretold that there would be this period of oppression (עָנָה [&apos;anah] in Gen 15:13). In other words, God had decreed and predicted both their becoming a great nation and the oppression to show that he could fulfill his promise to Abraham in spite of the bondage. 33 tn Heb &quot;they felt a loathing before/because of&quot;; the referent (the Egyptians) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
34 tn Heb &quot;the Egyptians.&quot; For stylistic reasons this has been replaced by the pronoun &quot;they&quot; in the translation. 35 tn Heb &quot;with rigor, oppression.&quot;

36 sn The verb מָרַר (marar) anticipates the introduction of the theme of bitterness in the instructions for the Passover. 37 tn The preposition bet (ב) in this verse has the instrumental use: &quot;by means of&quot; (see GKC 380 §119.o). 38 tn Heb &quot;and in all service.&quot; 39 tn The line could be more literally translated, &quot;All their service in which they served them [was] with rigor.&quot; This takes the referent of בָּהֶם (bahem) to be the Egyptians. The pronoun may also resume the reference to the kinds of service and so not be needed in English: &quot;All their service in which they served [was] with rigor.&quot;

40 tn Heb &quot;and the king of Egypt said.&quot; 41 sn The word for &quot;midwife&quot; is simply the Piel participle of the verb יָלַד (yalad, &quot;to give birth&quot;). So these were women who assisted in the childbirth process. It seems probable that given the number of the Israelites in the passage, these two women could not have been the only Hebrew midwives, but they may have been over the midwives (Rashi). Moreover, the LXX and Vulgate do not take &quot;Hebrew&quot; as an adjective, but as a genitive after the construct, yielding &quot;midwives of/over the Hebrews.&quot; This leaves open the possibility that these women were not Hebrews. This would solve the question of how the king ever expected Hebrew midwives to kill Hebrew children. And yet, the two women have Hebrew names. 42 tn Heb &quot;who the name of the first [was] Shiphrah, and the name of the second [was] Puah.&quot;

43 tn The verse starts with the verb that began the last verse; to read it again seems redundant. Some versions render it &quot;spoke&quot; in v. 15 and &quot;said&quot; in v. 16. In effect, Pharaoh has been delayed from speaking while the midwives are named. 44 tn The form is the Piel infinitive construct serving in an adverbial clause of time. This clause lays the foundation for the next verb, the Qal perfect with a vav consecutive: &quot;when you assist...then you will observe.&quot; The latter carries an instructional nuance (= the imperfect of instruction), &quot;you are to observe.&quot; 45 tn Heb &quot;at the birthstool&quot; (cf. ASV, NASB, NRSV), but since this particular item is not especially well known today, the present translation simply states &quot;at the delivery.&quot; Cf. NIV &quot;delivery stool.&quot; 46 sn The instructions must have been temporary or selective, otherwise the decree from the king would have ended the slave population of Hebrews. It is also possible that the king did not think through this, but simply took steps to limit the population growth. The narrative is not interested in supplying details, only in portraying the king as a wicked fool bent on destroying Israel. 47 tn The last form וָחָיָה (vakhaya) in the verse is unusual; rather than behaving as a III-Hey form, it is written as a geminate but without the daghesh forte in pause (GKC 218 §76.i). In the conditional clause, following the parallel instruction (&quot;kill him&quot;), this form should be rendered &quot;she may live&quot; or &quot;let her live.&quot;

48 tn Heb &quot;and they [fem. pl.] feared&quot;; the referent (the midwives) has been specified in the translation for clarity. 49 tn The verb is the Piel preterite of חָיָה (khaya, &quot;to live&quot;). The Piel often indicates a factitive nuance with stative verbs, showing the cause of the action. Here it means &quot;let live, cause to live.&quot; The verb is the exact opposite of Pharaoh&apos;s command for them to kill the boys.

50 tn The verb קָרָא (qara&apos;) followed by the lamed (ל) preposition has here the nuance of &quot;summon.&quot; The same construction is used later when Pharaoh summons Moses. 51 tn The second verb in Pharaoh&apos;s speech is a preterite with a vav (ו) consecutive. It may indicate a simple sequence: &quot;Why have you done...and (so that you) let live?&quot; It could also indicate that this is a second question, &quot;Why have you done ...[why] have you let live?&quot;

52 sn See further N. Lemche, &quot;&apos;Hebrew&apos; as a National Name for Israel,&quot; ST 33 (1979): 1-23. 53 tn Heb &quot;they&quot;; the referent (the Hebrew women) has been specified in the translation for clarity. 54 tn Heb &quot;before the midwife comes to them (and) they give birth.&quot; The perfect tense with the vav consecutive serves as the apodosis to the preceding temporal clause; it has the frequentative nuance (see GKC 337-38 §112.oo). sn The point of this brief section is that the midwives respected God above the king. They simply followed a higher authority that prohibited killing. Fearing God is a basic part of the true faith that leads to an obedient course of action and is not terrified by worldly threats. There probably was enough truth in what they were saying to be believable, but they clearly had no intention of honoring the king by participating in murder, and they saw no reason to give him a straightforward answer. God honored their actions.

55 tn The verb וַיֵּיטֶב (vayyetev) is the Hiphil preterite of יָטַב (yatav). In this stem the word means &quot;to cause good, treat well, treat favorably.&quot; The vav (ו) consecutive shows that this favor from God was a result of their fearing and obeying him.

56 tn The temporal indicator וַיְהִי (vayÿhi) focuses attention on the causal clause and lays the foundation for the main clause, namely, &quot;God made households for them.&quot; This is the second time the text affirms the reason for their defiance, their fear of God. 57 tn Or &quot;families&quot;; Heb &quot;houses.&quot;

58 tn The substantive כֹּל (kol) followed by the article stresses the entirety - &quot;all sons&quot; or &quot;all daughters&quot; - even though the nouns are singular in Hebrew (see GKC 411 §127.b). 59 tn The form includes a pronominal suffix that reiterates the object of the verb: &quot;every son...you will throw it.&quot; 60 tn The first imperfect has the force of a definite order, but the second, concerning the girls, could also have the nuance of permission, which may fit better. Pharaoh is simply allowing the girls to live. sn Verse 22 forms a fitting climax to the chapter, in which the king continually seeks to destroy the Israelite strength. Finally, with this decree, he throws off any subtlety and commands the open extermination of Hebrew males. The verse forms a transition to the next chapter, in which Moses is saved by Pharaoh&apos;s own daughter. These chapters show that the king&apos;s efforts to destroy the strength of Israel - so clearly a work of God - met with failure again and again. And that failure involved the efforts of women, whom Pharaoh did not consider a threat.

1 sn The chapter records the exceptional survival of Moses under the decree of death by Pharaoh (vv. 1-10), the flight of Moses from Pharaoh after killing the Egyptian (vv. 11-15), the marriage of Moses (vv. 16-22), and finally a note about the Lord&apos;s hearing the sighing of the people in bondage (vv. 23-25). The first part is the birth. The Bible has several stories about miraculous or special births and deliverances of those destined to lead Israel. Their impact is essentially to authenticate the individual&apos;s ministry. If the person&apos;s beginning was providentially provided and protected by the Lord, then the mission must be of divine origin too. In this chapter the plot works around the decree for the death of the children - a decree undone by the women. The second part of the chapter records Moses&apos; flight and marriage. Having introduced the deliverer Moses in such an auspicious way, the chapter then records how this deliverer acted presumptuously and had to flee for his life. Any deliverance God desired had to be supernatural, as the chapter&apos;s final note about answering prayer shows. 2 tn Heb &quot;house.&quot; In other words, the tribe of Levi. 3 tn Heb &quot;went and took&quot;; NASB &quot;went and married.&quot; 4 tn Heb &quot;a daughter of Levi.&quot; The word &quot;daughter&quot; is used in the sense of &quot;descendant&quot; and connects the new account with Pharaoh&apos;s command in 1:22. The words &quot;a woman who was&quot; are added for clarity in English. sn The first part of this section is the account of hiding the infant (vv. 1-4). The marriage, the birth, the hiding of the child, and the positioning of Miriam, are all faith operations that ignore the decree of Pharaoh or work around it to preserve the life of the child.

5 tn Or &quot;conceived&quot; (KJV, ASV, NAB, NASB, NRSV). 6 tn A preterite form with the vav consecutive can be subordinated to a following clause. What she saw stands as a reason for what she did: &quot;when she saw...she hid him three months.&quot; 7 tn After verbs of perceiving or seeing there are frequently two objects, the formal accusative (&quot;she saw him&quot;) and then a noun clause that explains what it was about the child that she perceived (&quot;that he was healthy&quot;). See GKC 365 §117.h. 8 tn Or &quot;fine&quot; (טוֹב, tov). The construction is parallel to phrases in the creation narrative (&quot;and God saw that it was good,&quot; Gen 1:4, 10, 12, 17, 21, 25, 31). B. Jacob says, &quot;She looked upon her child with a joy similar to that of God upon His creation (Gen 1.4ff.)&quot; (Exodus, 25).

9 sn See on the meaning of this basket C. Cohen, &quot;Hebrew tbh: Proposed Etymologies,&quot; JANESCU 9 (1972): 36-51. This term is used elsewhere only to refer to the ark of Noah. It may be connected to the Egyptian word for &quot;chest.&quot; 10 sn The circumstances of the saving of the child Moses have prompted several attempts by scholars to compare the material to the Sargon myth. See R. F. Johnson, IDB 3:440-50; for the text see L. W. King, Chronicles concerning Early Babylonian Kings, 2:87-90. Those who see the narrative using the Sargon story&apos;s pattern would be saying that the account presents Moses in imagery common to the ancient world&apos;s expectations of extraordinary achievement and deliverance. In the Sargon story the infant&apos;s mother set him adrift in a basket in a river; he was loved by the gods and destined for greatness. Saying Israel used this to invent the account in Exodus would undermine its reliability. But there are other difficulties with the Sargon comparison, not the least of which is the fact that the meaning and function of the Sargon story are unclear. Second, there is no outside threat to the child Sargon. The account simply shows how a child was exposed, rescued, nurtured, and became king (see B. S. Childs, Exodus [OTL], 8-12). Third, other details do not fit: Moses&apos; father is known, Sargon&apos;s is not; Moses is never abandoned, since he is never out of the care of his parents, and the finder is a princess and not a goddess. Moreover, without knowing the precise function and meaning of the Sargon story, it is almost impossible to explain its use as a pattern for the biblical account. By itself, the idea of a mother putting a child by the river if she wants him to be found would have been fairly sensible, for that is where the women of the town would be washing their clothes or bathing. If someone wanted to be sure the infant was discovered by a sympathetic woman, there would be no better setting (see R. A. Cole, Exodus [TOTC], 57). While there need not be a special genre of storytelling here, it is possible that Exodus 2 might have drawn on some of the motifs and forms of the other account to describe the actual event in the sparing of Moses - if they knew of it. If so it would show that Moses was cast in the form of the greats of the past.

Gen 16:12; 25:18). 3 sn &quot;Horeb&quot; is another name for Mount Sinai. There is a good deal of foreshadowing in this verse, for later Moses would shepherd the people of Israel and lead them to Mount Sinai to receive the Law. See D. Skinner, &quot;Some Major Themes of Exodus,&quot; Mid-America Theological Journal 1 (1977): 31-42.

4 sn The designation &quot;the angel of the Lord&quot; (Heb &quot;the angel of Yahweh&quot;) occurred in Genesis already (16:7-13; 21:17; 22:11-18). There is some ambiguity in the expression, but it seems often to be interchangeable with God&apos;s name itself, indicating that it refers to the Lord. 5 tn The verb וַיֵּרָא (vayyera&apos;) is the Niphal preterite of the verb &quot;to see.&quot; For similar examples of רָאָה (ra&apos;ah) in Niphal where the subject &quot;appears,&quot; that is, allows himself to be seen, or presents himself, see Gen 12:7; 35:9; 46:29; Exod 6:3; and 23:17. B. Jacob notes that God appears in this way only to individuals and never to masses of people; it is his glory that appears to the masses (Exodus, 49). 6 tn Gesenius rightly classifies this as a bet (ב) essentiae (GKC 379 §119.i); it would then indicate that Yahweh appeared to Moses &quot;as a flame.&quot; 7 sn Fire frequently accompanies the revelation of Yahweh in Exodus as he delivers Israel, guides her, and purifies her. The description here is unique, calling attention to the manifestation as a flame of fire from within the bush. However, in this revelation the fire is coming from within the bush, not from outside, and it represents the Lord who will deliver his people from persecution. See further E. This was the amazing thing, for nothing would burn faster in the desert than a thornbush on fire.

11 tn Heb &quot;And Moses said.&quot; The implication is that Moses said this to himself. 12 tn The construction uses the cohortative אָסֻרָה־נָּא (&apos;asura-nna&apos;) followed by an imperfect with vav (וְאֶרְאֶה, vÿ&apos;er&apos;eh) to express the purpose or result (logical sequence): &quot;I will turn aside in order that I may see.&quot; 13 tn Heb &quot;great.&quot; The word means something extraordinary here. In using this term Moses revealed his reaction to the strange sight and his anticipation that something special was about to happen. So he turned away from the flock to investigate. 14 tn The verb is an imperfect. Here it has the progressive nuance - the bush is not burning up.

1 sn In chap. 3, the first part of this extensive call, Yahweh promises to deliver his people. At the hesitancy of Moses, God guarantees his presence will be with him, and that assures the success of the mission. But with chap. 4, the second half of the call, the tone changes sharply. Now Moses protests his inadequacies in view of the nature of the task. In many ways, these verses address the question, &quot;Who is sufficient for these things?&quot; There are three basic movements in the passage. The first nine verses tell how God gave Moses signs in case Israel did not believe him (4:1-9). The second section records how God dealt with the speech problem of Moses (4:10-12). And finally, the last section records God&apos;s provision of a helper, someone who could talk well (4:13-17). See also J. E. Hamlin, &quot;The Liberator&apos;s Ordeal: A Study of Exodus 4:1-9,&quot; Rhetorical Criticism [PTMS], 33-42. 2 tn Heb &quot;and Moses answered and said.&quot; 3 tn Or &quot;What if.&quot; The use of הֵן (hen) is unusual here, introducing a conditional idea in the question without a following consequence clause (see Exod 8:22 HT [8:26 ET]; Jer 2:10; 2 Chr 7:13). The Greek has &quot;if not&quot; but adds the clause &quot;what shall I say to them?&quot; 4 tn Heb &quot;listen to my voice,&quot; so as to respond positively.

5 tn Or &quot;rod&quot; (KJV, ASV); NCV, CEV &quot;walking stick&quot;; NLT &quot;shepherd&apos;s staff.&quot; sn The staff appears here to be the shepherd&apos;s staff that he was holding. It now will become the instrument with which Moses will do the mighty works, for it is the medium of the display of the divine power (S. R. Driver, Exodus, 27; also, L. Shalit, &quot;How Moses Turned a Staff into a Snake and Back Again,&quot; BAR 9 [1983]: 72-73).

6 tn Heb &quot;he&quot;; the referent (the Lord) has been specified in the translation for clarity. 7 sn The details of the verse are designed to show that there was a staff that became a snake. The question is used to affirm that there truly was a staff, and then the report of Moses running from it shows it was a genuine snake. Using the serpent as a sign would have had an impact on the religious ideas of Egypt, for the sacred cobra was one of their symbols.

1 sn The enthusiasm of the worshipers in the preceding chapter turns sour in this one when Pharaoh refuses to cooperate. The point is clear that when the people of God attempt to devote their full service and allegiance to God, they encounter opposition from the world. Rather than finding instant blessing and peace, they find conflict. This is the theme that will continue through the plague narratives. But what makes chapter 5 especially interesting is how the people reacted to this opposition. The chapter has three sections: first, the confrontation between Moses and Pharaoh (vv. 1-5); then the report of the stern opposition of the king (vv. 6-14); and finally, the sad account of the effect of this opposition on the people (vv. 15-21). 2 tn Heb &quot;Yahweh.&quot; 3 tn The form שַׁלַּח (shallakh), the Piel imperative, has been traditionally translated &quot;let [my people] go.&quot; The Qal would be &quot;send&quot;; so the Piel &quot;send away, release, dismiss, discharge.&quot; B. Jacob observes, &quot;If a person was dismissed through the use of this verb, then he ceased to be within the power or sphere of influence of the individual who had dismissed him. He was completely free and subsequently acted entirely on his own responsibility&quot; (Exodus, 115). 4 tn The verb חָגַג (khagag) means to hold a feast or to go on a pilgrim feast. The Arabic cognate of the noun form is haj, best known for the pilgrim flight of Mohammed, the hajira. The form in the text (וְיָחֹגּוּ, vÿyakhoggu) is subordinated to the imperative and thus shows the purpose of the imperative.

5 tn Heb &quot;Yahweh.&quot; This is a rhetorical question, expressing doubt or indignation or simply a negative thought that Yahweh is nothing (see erotesis in E. W. Bullinger, Figures of Speech, 944-45). Pharaoh is not asking for information (cf. 1 Sam 25:5-10). 6 tn The relative pronoun introduces the consecutive clause that depends on the interrogative clause (see GKC 318-19 §107.u). 7 tn The imperfect tense here receives the classification of obligatory imperfect. The verb שָׁמַע (shama&apos;) followed by &quot;in the voice of&quot; is idiomatic; rather than referring to simple audition - &quot;that I should hear his voice&quot; - it conveys the thought of listening that issues in action - &quot;that I should obey him.&quot; sn The construction of these clauses is similar to (ironically) the words of Moses: &quot;Who am I that I should go?&quot; (3:11). 8 tn The Piel infinitive construct here has the epexegetical usage with lamed (ל); it explains the verb &quot;obey.&quot; 9 sn This absolute statement of Pharaoh is part of a motif that will develop throughout the conflict. For Pharaoh, the Lord (Yahweh) did not exist. So he said &quot;I do not know the Lord [i.e., Yahweh].&quot; The point of the plagues and the exodus will be &quot;that he might know.&quot; Pharaoh will come to know this Yahweh, but not in any pleasant way.

10 tn The word &quot;journey&quot; is an adverbial accusative telling the distance that Moses wanted the people to go. It is qualified by &quot;three days.&quot; It is not saying that they will be gone three days, but that they will go a distance that will take three days to cover (see Gen 31:22-23; Num 10:33; 33:8). 11 tn The purpose clause here is formed with a second cohortative joined with a vav (ו): &quot;let us go...and let us sacrifice.&quot; The purpose of the going was to sacrifice. sn Where did Moses get the idea that they should have a pilgrim feast and make sacrifices? God had only said they would serve Him in that mountain. In the OT the pilgrim feasts to the sanctuary three times a year incorporated the ideas of serving the Lord and keeping the commands. So the words here use the more general idea of appearing before their God. They would go to the desert because there was no homeland yet. Moses later spoke of the journey as necessary to avoid offending Egyptian sensibilities (8:25-26). 12 sn The last clause of this verse is rather unexpected here: &quot;lest he meet [afflict] us with pestilence or sword.&quot; To fail to comply with the summons of one&apos;s God was to invite such calamities. The Law would later incorporate many such things as the curses for disobedience. Moses is indicating to Pharaoh that there is more reason to fear Yahweh than Pharaoh.

1 sn The expression &quot;I will do to Pharaoh&quot; always refers to the plagues. God would first show his sovereignty over Pharaoh before defeating him. 2 tn The expression &quot;with a strong hand&quot; (וּבְיָד חֲזָקָה, uvÿyad khazaqah) could refer (1) to God&apos;s powerful intervention (&quot;compelled by my strong hand&quot;) or (2) to Pharaoh&apos;s forceful pursuit (&quot;he will forcefully drive them out&quot;). In Exod 3:20 God has summarized what his hand would do in Egypt, and that is probably what is intended here, as he promises that Moses will see what God will do. All Egypt ultimately desired that Israel be released (12:33), and when they were released Pharaoh pursued them to the sea, and so in a sense drove them out - whether that was his intention or not. But ultimately it was God&apos;s power that was the real force behind it all. U. Cassuto (Exodus, 74) considers that it is unlikely that the phrase would be used in the same verse twice with the same meaning. So he thinks that the first &quot;strong hand&quot; is God&apos;s, and the second &quot;strong hand&quot; is Pharaoh&apos;s. It is true that if Pharaoh acted forcefully in any way that contributed to Israel leaving Egypt it was because God was acting forcefully in his life. So in an understated way, God is saying that when forced by God&apos;s strong hand, Pharaoh will indeed release God&apos;s people.&quot; 3 tn Or &quot;and he will forcefully drive them out of his land,&quot; if the second occurrence of &quot;strong hand&quot; refers to Pharaoh&apos;s rather than God&apos;s (see the previous note). sn In Exod 12:33 the Egyptians were eager to send (release) Israel away in haste, because they all thought they were going to die.

4 tn Heb &quot;And God spoke.&quot; 5 sn The announcement &quot;I am the Lord&quot; (Heb &quot;Yahweh&quot;) draws in the preceding revelation in Exod 3:15. In that place God called Moses to this task and explained the significance of the name &quot;Yahweh&quot; by the enigmatic expression &quot;I am that I am.&quot; &quot;I am&quot; (אֶהְיֶה, &apos;ehyeh) is not a name; &quot;Yahweh&quot; is. But the explanation of the name with this sentence indicates that Yahweh is the one who is always there, and that guarantees the future, for everything he does is consistent with his nature. He is eternal, never changing; he remains. Now, in Exodus 6, the meaning of the name &quot;Yahweh&quot; will be more fully unfolded.

6 tn The preposition bet (ב) in this construction should be classified as a bet essentiae, a bet of essence (see also GKC 379 §119.i). 7 tn The traditional rendering of the title as &quot;Almighty&quot; is reflected in LXX and Jerome. But there is still little agreement on the etymology and exact meaning of אֵל־שַׁדַּי (&apos;el-shadday). Suggestions have included the idea of &quot;mountain God,&quot; meaning the high God, as well as &quot;the God with breasts.&quot; But there is very little evidence supporting such conclusions and not much reason to question the ancient versions. 8 tn The noun שְׁמִי (shÿmi, &quot;my name,&quot; and &quot;Yahweh&quot; in apposition to it), is an adverbial accusative, specifying how the patriarchs &quot;knew&quot; him. 9 tn Heb &quot;Yahweh,&quot; traditionally rendered in English as &quot;the Lord.&quot; The phrase has been placed in quotation marks in the translation to indicate it represents the tetragrammaton. 10 tn The verb is the Niphal form נוֹדַעְתִּי (noda&apos;ti). If the text had wanted to say, &quot;I did not make myself known,&quot; then a Hiphil form would have been more likely. It is saying, &quot;but by my name Yahweh I was not known to them.&quot; sn There are a number of important issues that need clarification in the interpretation of this section. First, it is important to note that &quot;I am Yahweh&quot; is not a new revelation of a previously unknown name. It would be introduced differently if it were. This is the identification of the covenant God as the one calling Moses - that would be proof for the people that their God had called him. Second, the title &quot;El Shadday&quot; is not a name, but a title. It is true that in the patriarchal accounts &quot;El Shadday&quot; is used six times; in Job it is used thirty times. Many conclude that it does reflect the idea of might or power. In some of those passages that reveal God as &quot;El Shadday,&quot; the name &quot;Yahweh&quot; was also used. But Wellhausen and other proponents of the earlier source critical analysis used Exod 6:3 to say that P, the so-called priestly source, was aware that the name &quot;Yahweh&quot; was not known by them, even though J, the supposed Yahwistic source, wrote using the name as part of his theology. Third, the texts of Genesis show that Yahweh had appeared to the patriarchs (Gen 12:1, 17:1, 18:1, 26:2, 26:24, 26:12, 35:1, 48:3), and that he spoke to each one of them (Gen 12:7, 15:1, 26:2, 28:13, 31:3). The name &quot;Yahweh&quot; occurs 162 times in Genesis, 34 of those times on the lips of speakers in Genesis (W. C. Kaiser, Jr., &quot;Exodus,&quot; EBC 2:340-41). They also made proclamation of Yahweh by name (4:26, 12:8), and they named places with the name (22:14). These passages should not be ignored or passed off as later interpretation. Fourth, &quot;Yahweh&quot; is revealed as the God of power, the sovereign God, who was true to his word and could be believed. He would do as he said (Num 23:19; 14:35; Exod 12:25; 22:24; 24:14; 36:36; 37:14). Fifth, there is a difference between promise and fulfillment in the way revelation is apprehended. The patriarchs were individuals who received the promises but without the fulfillment. The fulfillment could only come after the Israelites became a nation. Now, in Egypt, they are ready to become that promised nation. The two periods were not distinguished by not having and by having the name, but by two ways God revealed the significance of his name. &quot;I am Yahweh&quot; to the patriarchs indicated that he was the absolute, almighty, eternal God. The patriarchs were individuals sojourning in the land. God appeared to them in the significance of El Shadday. That was not his name. So Gen 17:1 says that &quot;Yahweh appeared...and said, &apos;I am El Shadday.&apos;&quot; See also Gen 35:11, 48:2, 28:3. Sixth, the verb &quot;to know&quot; is never used to introduce a name which had never been known or experienced. The Niphal and Hiphil of the verb are used only to describe the recognition of the overtones or significance of the name (see Jer 16:21, Isa 52:6; Ps 83:17ff; 1 Kgs 8:41ff. [people will know his name when prayers are answered]). For someone to say that he knew Yahweh meant that Yahweh had been experienced or recognized (see Exod 33:6; 1 Kgs 18:36; Jer 28:9; and Ps 76:2). Seventh, &quot;Yahweh&quot; is not one of God&apos;s names - it is his only name. Other titles, like &quot;El Shadday,&quot; are not strictly names but means of revealing Yahweh. All the revelations to the patriarchs could not compare to this one, because God was now dealing with the nation. He would make his name known to them through his deeds (see Ezek 20:5). So now they will &quot;know&quot; the &quot;name.&quot; The verb יָדַע (yada&apos;) means more than &quot;aware of, be knowledgeable about&quot;; it means &quot;to experience&quot; the reality of the revelation by that name. This harmonizes with the usage of שֵׁם (shem), &quot;name,&quot; which encompasses all the attributes and actions of God. It is not simply a reference to a title, but to the way that God revealed himself - God gave meaning to his name through his acts. God is not saying that he had not revealed a name to the patriarchs (that would have used the Hiphil of the verb). Rather, he is saying that the patriarchs did not experience what the name Yahweh actually meant, and they could not without seeing it fulfilled. When Moses came to the elders, he identified his call as from Yahweh, the God of the fathers - and they accepted him. They knew the name. But, when they were delivered from bondage, then they fully knew by experience what that name meant, for his promises were fulfilled. U. Cassuto (Exodus, 79) paraphrases it this way: &quot;I revealed Myself to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in My aspect that finds expression in the name Shaddai...I was not known to them, that is, it was not given to them to recognize Me as One that fulfils his promises.&quot; This generation was about to &quot;know&quot; the name that their ancestors knew and used, but never experienced with the fulfillment of the promises. This section of Exodus confirms this interpretation, because in it God promised to bring them out of Egypt and give them the promised land - then they would know that he is Yahweh (6:7). This meaning should have been evident from its repetition to the Egyptians throughout the plagues - that they might know Yahweh (e.g., 7:5). See further R. D. Wilson, &quot;Yahweh [Jehovah] and Exodus 6:3,&quot; Classical Evangelical Essays in Old Testament Interpretation, 29-40; L. A. Herrboth, &quot;Exodus 6:3b: Was God Known to the Patriarchs as Jehovah?&quot; CTM 4 (1931): 345-49; F. C. Smith, &quot;Observation on the Use of the Names and Titles of God in Genesis,&quot; EvQ 40 (1968): 103-9.

1 tn The word &quot;like&quot; is added for clarity, making explicit the implied comparison in the statement &quot;I have made you God to Pharaoh.&quot; The word אֱלֹהִים (&apos;elohim) is used a few times in the Bible for humans (e.g., Pss 45:6; 82:1), and always clearly in the sense of a subordinate to GOD - they are his representatives on earth. The explanation here goes back to 4:16. If Moses is like God in that Aaron is his prophet, then Moses is certainly like God to Pharaoh. Only Moses, then, is able to speak to Pharaoh with such authority, giving him commands. 2 tn The word נְבִיאֶךָ (nÿvi&apos;ekha, &quot;your prophet&quot;) recalls 4:16. Moses was to be like God to Aaron, and Aaron was to speak for him. This indicates that the idea of a &quot;prophet&quot; was of one who spoke for God, an idea with which Moses and Aaron and the readers of Exodus are assumed to be familiar.

3 tn The imperfect tense here should have the nuance of instruction or injunction: &quot;you are to speak.&quot; The subject is singular (Moses) and made emphatic by the presence of the personal pronoun &quot;you.&quot; 4 tn The phrase translated &quot;everything I command you&quot; is a noun clause serving as the direct object of the verb &quot;speak.&quot; The verb in the clause (אֲצַוֶּךָ, &apos;atsavvekha) is the Piel imperfect. It could be classified as a future: &quot;everything that I will command you.&quot; A nuance of progressive imperfect also fits well: &quot;everything that I am commanding you.&quot; sn The distinct emphasis is important. Aaron will speak to the people and Pharaoh what Moses tells him, and Moses will speak to Aaron what God commands him. The use of &quot;command&quot; keeps everything in perspective for Moses&apos; position. 5 tn The form is וְשִׁלַּח (vÿshillakh), a Piel perfect with vav (ו) consecutive. Following the imperfects of injunction or instruction, this verb continues the sequence. It could be taken as equal to an imperfect expressing future (&quot;and he will release&quot;) or subordinate to express purpose (&quot;to release&quot; = &quot;in order that he may release&quot;).

6 tn The clause begins with the emphatic use of the pronoun and a disjunctive vav (ו) expressing the contrast &quot;But as for me, I will harden.&quot; They will speak, but God will harden. sn The imperfect tense of the verb קָשָׁה (qasha) is found only here in these &quot;hardening passages.&quot; The verb (here the Hiphil for &quot;I will harden&quot;) summarizes Pharaoh&apos;s resistance to what God would be doing through Moses - he would stubbornly resist and refuse to submit; he would be resolved in his opposition. See R. R. Wilson, &quot;The Hardening of Pharaoh&apos;s Heart,&quot; CBQ 41 (1979): 18-36. 7 tn The form beginning the second half of the verse is the perfect tense with vav (ו) consecutive, הִרְבֵּיתִי (hirbeti). It could be translated as a simple future in sequence after the imperfect preceding it, but the logical connection is not obvious. Since it carries the force of an imperfect due to the sequence, it may be subordinated as a temporal clause to the next clause that begins in v. 4. That maintains the flow of the argument.

1 sn Beginning with 8:1, the verse numbers through 8:32 in English Bibles differ from the verse numbers in the Hebrew text (BHS), with 8:1 ET = 7:26 HT, 8:2 ET = 7:27 HT, 8:3 ET = 7:28 HT, 8:4 ET = 7:29 HT, 8:5 ET = 8:1 HT, etc., through 8:32 ET = 8:28 HT. Thus in English Bibles chapter 8 has 32 verses, while in the Hebrew Bible it has 28 verses, with the four extra verses attached to chapter 7.

2 tn The construction here uses the deictic particle and the participle to convey the imminent future: &quot;I am going to plague/about to plague.&quot; The verb נָגַף (nagaf) means &quot;to strike, to smite,&quot; and its related noun means &quot;a blow, a plague, pestilence&quot; or the like. For Yahweh to say &quot;I am about to plague you&quot; could just as easily mean &quot;I am about to strike you.&quot; That is why these &quot;plagues&quot; can be described as &quot;blows&quot; received from God. 3 tn Heb &quot;plague all your border with frogs.&quot; The expression &quot;all your border&quot; is figurative for all the territory of Egypt and the people and things that are within the borders (also used in Exod 10:4, 14, 19; 13:7). sn This word for frogs is mentioned in the OT only in conjunction with this plague (here and Pss 78:45, 105:30). R. A. Cole (Exodus [TOTC], 91) suggests that this word &quot;frogs&quot; (צְפַרְדְּעִים, tsÿfardÿ&apos;im) may be an onomatopoeic word, something like &quot;croakers&quot;; it is of Egyptian origin and could be a Hebrew attempt to write the Arabic dofda.

4 sn The choice of this verb שָׁרַץ (sharats) recalls its use in the creation account (Gen 1:20). The water would be swarming with frogs in abundance. There is a hint here of this being a creative work of God as well. 5 sn This verse lists places the frogs will go. The first three are for Pharaoh personally - they are going to touch his private life. Then the text mentions the servants and the people. Mention of the ovens and kneading bowls (or troughs) of the people indicates that food would be contaminated and that it would be impossible even to eat a meal in peace.

1 sn This plague demonstrates that Yahweh has power over the livestock of Egypt. He is able to strike the animals with disease and death, thus delivering a blow to the economic as well as the religious life of the land. By the former plagues many of the Egyptian religious ceremonies would have been interrupted and objects of veneration defiled or destroyed. Now some of the important deities will be attacked. In Goshen, where the cattle are merely cattle, no disease hits, but in the rest of Egypt it is a different matter. Osiris, the savior, cannot even save the brute in which his own soul is supposed to reside. Apis and Mnevis, the ram of Ammon, the sheep of Sais, and the goat of Mendes, perish together. Hence, Moses reminds Israel afterward, &quot;On their gods also Yahweh executed judgments&quot; (Num 33:4). When Jethro heard of all these events, he said, &quot;Now I know that Yahweh is greater than all the gods&quot; (Exod 18:11).

2 tn The object &quot;them&quot; is implied in the context. 3 tn עוֹד (&apos;od), an adverb meaning &quot;yet, still,&quot; can be inflected with suffixes and used as a predicator of existence, with the nuance &quot;to still be, yet be&quot; (T. O. Lambdin, Introduction to Biblical Hebrew, 171-72, §137). Then, it is joined here with the Hiphil participle מַחֲזִיק (makhaziq) to form the sentence &quot;you are still holding them.&quot;

4 tn The form used here is הוֹיָה (hoyah), the Qal active participle, feminine singular, from the verb &quot;to be.&quot; This is the only place in the OT that this form occurs. Ogden shows that this form is appropriate with the particle הִנֵּה (hinneh) to stress impending divine action, and that it conforms to the pattern in these narratives where five times the participle is used in the threat to Pharaoh (7:17; 8:2; 9:3, 14; 10:4). See G. S. Ogden, &quot;Notes on the Use of הויה in Exodus IX. 3,&quot; VT 17 (1967): 483-84. 5 tn The word דֶּבֶר (dever) is usually translated &quot;pestilence&quot; when it applies to diseases for humans. It is used only here and in Ps 78:50 for animals. 6 sn The older view that camels were not domesticated at this time (S. R. Driver, Exodus, 70; W. F. Albright, Archaeology and the Religion of Israel, 96; et. al.) has been corrected by more recently uncovered information (see K. A. Kitchen, NBD3 160-61).

1 sn The Egyptians dreaded locusts like every other ancient civilization. They had particular gods to whom they looked for help in such catastrophes. The locust-scaring deities of Greece and Asia were probably looked to in Egypt as well (especially in view of the origins in Egypt of so many of those religious ideas). The announcement of the plague falls into the now-familiar pattern. God tells Moses to go and speak to Pharaoh but reminds Moses that he has hardened his heart. Yahweh explains that he has done this so that he might show his power, so that in turn they might declare his name from generation to generation. This point is stressed so often that it must not be minimized. God was laying the foundation of the faith for Israel - the sovereignty of Yahweh. 2 tn Heb &quot;and Yahweh said.&quot; 3 tn The verb is שִׁתִי (shiti, &quot;I have put&quot;); it is used here as a synonym for the verb שִׂים (sim). Yahweh placed the signs in his midst, where they will be obvious. 4 tn Heb &quot;in his midst.&quot;

5 tn The expression is unusual: תְּסַפֵּר בְּאָזְנֵי (tÿsapper bÿ&apos;ozne, &quot;[that] you may declare in the ears of&quot;). The clause explains an additional reason for God&apos;s hardening the heart of Pharaoh, namely, so that the Israelites can tell their children of God&apos;s great wonders. The expression is highly poetic and intense - like Ps 44:1, which says, &quot;we have heard with our ears.&quot; The emphasis would be on the clear teaching, orally, from one generation to another. 6 tn The verb הִתְעַלַּלְתִּי (hit&apos;allalti) is a bold anthropomorphism. The word means to occupy oneself at another&apos;s expense, to toy with someone, which may be paraphrased with &quot;mock.&quot; The whole point is that God is shaming and disgracing Egypt, making them look foolish in their arrogance and stubbornness (W. C. Kaiser, Jr., &quot;Exodus,&quot; EBC 2:366-67). Some prefer to translate it as &quot;I have dealt ruthlessly&quot; with Egypt (see U. Cassuto, Exodus, 123). 7 tn Heb &quot;of Egypt.&quot; The place is put by metonymy for the inhabitants. 8 tn The word &quot;about&quot; is supplied to clarify this as another object of the verb &quot;declare.&quot; 9 tn Heb &quot;put&quot; or &quot;placed.&quot; 10 tn The form is the perfect tense with vav consecutive, וִידַעְתֶּם (vida&apos;tem, &quot;and that you might know&quot;). This provides another purpose for God&apos;s dealings with Egypt in the way that he was doing. The form is equal to the imperfect tense with vav (ו) prefixed; it thus parallels the imperfect that began v. 2 - &quot;that you might tell.&quot;

11 tn The verb is מֵאַנְתָּ (me&apos;anta), a Piel perfect. After &quot;how long,&quot; the form may be classified as present perfect (&quot;how long have you refused), for it describes actions begun previously but with the effects continuing. (See GKC 311 §106.g-h). The use of a verb describing a state or condition may also call for a present translation (&quot;how long do you refuse&quot;) that includes past, present, and potentially future, in keeping with the question &quot;how long.&quot; 12 tn The clause is built on the use of the infinitive construct to express the direct object of the verb - it answers the question of what Pharaoh was refusing to do. The Niphal infinitive construct (note the elision of the ה [hey] prefix after the preposition [see GKC 139 §51.l]) is from the verb עָנָה (&apos;anah). The verb in this stem would mean &quot;humble oneself.&quot; The question is somewhat rhetorical, since God was not yet through humbling Pharaoh, who would not humble himself. The issue between Yahweh and Pharaoh is deeper than simply whether or not Pharaoh will let the Israelites leave Egypt.

1 sn The last plague is the most severe; it is that for which all the others were preliminary warnings. Up to this point Yahweh had been showing his power to destroy Pharaoh, and now he would begin to do so by bringing death to the Egyptians, a death that would fulfill the warning of talionic judgment - &quot;let my son go, or I will kill your son.&quot; The passage records the announcement of the judgment first to Moses and then through Moses to Pharaoh. The first two verses record the word of God to Moses. This is followed by a parenthetical note about how God had elevated Moses and Israel in the eyes of Egypt (v. 3). Then there is the announcement to Pharaoh (vv. 4-8). This is followed by a parenthetical note on how God had hardened Pharaoh so that Yahweh would be elevated over him. It is somewhat problematic here that Moses is told not to see Pharaoh&apos;s face again. On the one hand, given the nature of Pharaoh to blow hot and cold and to change his mind, it is not impossible for another meeting to have occurred. But Moses said he would not do it (v. 29). One solution some take is to say that the warning in 10:28 originally stood after chapter 11. A change like that is unwarranted, and without support. It may be that vv. 1-3 are parenthetical, so that the announcement in v. 4 follows closely after 10:29 in the chronology. The instruction to Moses in 11:1 might then have been given before he left Pharaoh or even before the interview in 10:24-29 took place. Another possibility, supported by usage in Akkadian, is that the expression &quot;see my face&quot; (and in v. 29 &quot;see your face&quot;) has to do with seeking to have an official royal audience (W. H. C. Propp, Exodus 1-18 [AB], 342). Pharaoh thinks that he is finished with Moses, but as 11:8 describes, Moses expects that in fact Moses will soon be the one in a position like that of royalty granting an audience to Egyptians. 2 tn The expression כְּשַּׂלְּחוֹ כָּלָה (kÿsallÿkho kalah) is difficult. It seems to say, &quot;as/when he releases [you] altogether.&quot; The LXX has &quot;and when he sends you forth with everything.&quot; Tg. Onq. and modern translators make kala adverbial, &quot;completely&quot; or &quot;altogether.&quot; B. S. Childs follows an emendation to read, &quot;as one sends away a bride&quot; (Exodus [OTL], 130). W. C. Kaiser prefers the view of Yaron that would render it &quot;in the manner of one&apos;s sending away a kallah [a slave purchased to be one&apos;s daughter-in-law]&quot; (&quot;Exodus,&quot; EBC 2:370). The last two readings call for revising the vocalization and introducing a rare word into the narrative. The simplest approach is to follow a meaning &quot;when he releases [you] altogether,&quot; i.e., with all your people and your livestock. 3 tn The words are emphatic: גָּרֵשׁ יְגָרֵשׁ (garesh yÿgaresh). The Piel verb means &quot;to drive out, expel.&quot; With the infinitive absolute it says that Pharaoh &quot;will drive you out vigorously.&quot; He will be glad to be rid of you - it will be a total expulsion.

4 tn Heb &quot;Speak now in the ears of the people.&quot; The expression is emphatic; it seeks to ensure that the Israelites hear the instruction. 5 tn The verb translated &quot;request&quot; is וְיִשְׁאֲלוּ (vÿyish&apos;alu), the Qal jussive: &quot;let them ask.&quot; This is the point introduced in Exod 3:22. The meaning of the verb might be stronger than simply &quot;ask&quot;; it might have something of the idea of &quot;implore&quot; (see also its use in the naming of Samuel, who was &quot;asked&quot; from Yahweh [1 Sam 1:20]). 6 tn &quot;each man is to request from his neighbor and each woman from her neighbor.&quot; sn Here neighbor refers to Egyptian neighbors, who are glad to see them go (12:33) and so willingly give their jewelry and vessels. 7 sn See D. Skinner, &quot;Some Major Themes of Exodus,&quot; Mid-America Theological Journal 1 (1977): 31-42.

8 tn Heb &quot;in the eyes of.&quot; 9 tn Heb &quot;in the eyes of the servants of Pharaoh and in the eyes of the people.&quot; In the translation the word &quot;Egyptian&quot; has been supplied to clarify that the Egyptians and not the Israelites are meant here. sn The presence of this clause about Moses, which is parenthetical in nature, further indicates why the Egyptians gave rather willingly to the Israelites. They were impressed by Moses&apos; miracles and his power with Pharaoh. Moses was great in stature - powerful and influential.

1 sn Chapter 12 details the culmination of the ten plagues on Egypt and the beginning of the actual deliverance from bondage. Moreover, the celebration of this festival of Passover was to become a central part of the holy calendar of Israel. The contents of this chapter have significance for NT studies as well, since the Passover was a type of the death of Jesus. The structure of this section before the crossing of the sea is as follows: the institution of the Passover (12:1-28), the night of farewell and departure (12:29-42), slaves and strangers (12:43-51), and the laws of the firstborn (13:1-16). In this immediate section there is the institution of the Passover itself (12:1-13), then the Unleavened Bread (12:14-20), and then the report of the response of the people (12:21-28). 2 tn Heb &quot;and Yahweh said.&quot; 3 tn Heb &quot;saying.&quot;

4 sn B. Jacob (Exodus, 294-95) shows that the intent of the passage was not to make this month in the spring the New Year - that was in the autumn. Rather, when counting months this was supposed to be remembered first, for it was the great festival of freedom from Egypt. He observes how some scholars have unnecessarily tried to date one New Year earlier than the other.

1 sn This next section seems a little confusing at first glance: vv. 1 and 2 call for the dedication of the firstborn, then vv. 3-10 instruct concerning the ritual of the Feast of Unleavened Bread, and then vv. 11-16 return to the firstborn. B. Jacob (Exodus, 360) explains that vv. 3-16 contain a sermon, in which Moses &quot;began his speech by reminding the people of the events which had just occurred and how they would be recalled by them in the future,&quot; and then he explained the rulings that went along with it. So the first two verses state the core of the sermon, a new command calling for the redeemed (firstborn) to be sanctified. The second portion stresses that God requires the redeemed to remember their redemption by purifying themselves (3-10). The third section (11-16) develops the theme of dedication to Yahweh. The point is that in view of God&apos;s mighty redemption, the redeemed (represented by the firstborn) must be set apart for Yahweh&apos;s service. 2 tn Heb &quot;and Yahweh spoke.&quot;

3 tn The verb &quot;sanctify&quot; is the Piel imperative of קָדַשׁ (qadash). In the Qal stem it means &quot;be holy, be set apart, be distinct,&quot; and in this stem &quot;sanctify, set apart.&quot; sn Here is the central principle of the chapter - the firstborn were sacred to God and must be &quot;set apart&quot; (the meaning of the verb &quot;sanctify&quot;) for his use. 4 tn The word פֶּטֶּר (petter) means &quot;that which opens&quot;; this construction literally says, &quot;that which opens every womb,&quot; which means &quot;the first offspring of every womb.&quot; Verses 12 and 15 further indicate male offspring. 5 tn Heb &quot;to me it.&quot; The preposition here expresses possession; the construction is simply &quot;it [is, belongs] to me.&quot;

6 tn The form is the infinitive absolute of זָכַר (zakhar, &quot;remember&quot;). The use of this form in place of the imperative (also found in the Decalogue with the Sabbath instruction) stresses the basic meaning of the root word, everything involved with remembering (emphatic imperative, according to GKC 346 §113.bb). The verb usually implies that there will be proper action based on what was remembered. sn There is a pattern in the arrangement of vv. 3-10 and 11-16. Both sections contain commands based on the mighty deliverance as reminders of the deliverance. &quot;With a mighty hand&quot; occurs in vv. 3, 9, 14, 16. An explanation to the son is found in vv. 8 and 14. The emphases &quot;sign on your hand&quot; and &quot;between your eyes&quot; are part of the conclusions to both halves (vv. 9, 16). 7 tn Heb &quot;from a house of slaves.&quot; &quot;House&quot; is obviously not meant to be literal; it indicates a location characterized by slavery, a land of slaves, as if they were in a slave house. Egypt is also called an &quot;iron-smelting furnace&quot; (Deut 4:20). 8 tn Heb &quot;from this&quot; [place]. 9 tn The verb is a Niphal imperfect; it could be rendered &quot;must not be eaten&quot; in the nuance of the instruction or injunction category, but permission fits this sermonic presentation very well - nothing with yeast may be eaten.

1 sn This chapter is a song of praise sung by Moses and the people right after the deliverance from the Sea. The song itself is vv. 1b-18; it falls into three sections - praise to God (1b-3), the cause for the praise (4-13), and the conclusion (14-18). The point of the first section is that God&apos;s saving acts inspire praise from his people; the second is that God&apos;s powerful acts deliver his people from the forces of evil; and the third section is that God&apos;s demonstrations of his sovereignty inspire confidence in him by his people. So the Victory Song is very much like the other declarative praise psalms - the resolve to praise, the power of God, the victory over the enemies, the incomparability of God in his redemption, and the fear of the people. See also C. Cohen, &quot;Studies in Early Israelite Poetry I: An Unrecognized Case of Three Line Staircase Parallelism in the Song of the Sea,&quot; JANESCU 7 (1975): 13-17; D. N. Freedman, &quot;Strophe and Meter in Exodus 15,&quot; A Light unto My Path, 163-203; E. Levine, &quot;Neofiti I: A Study of Exodus 15,&quot; Bib 54 (1973): 301-30; T. C. Butler, &quot;&apos;The Song of the Sea&apos;: Exodus 15:1-18: A Study in the Exegesis of Hebrew Poetry,&quot; DissAb 32 (1971): 2782-A. 2 tn The verb is יָשִׁיר (yashir), a normal imperfect tense form. But after the adverb &quot;then&quot; this form is to be treated as a preterite (see GKC 314-15 §107.c). 3 tn Heb &quot;and they said, saying.&quot; This has been simplified in the translation for stylistic reasons. 4 tn The form is the singular cohortative, expressing the resolution of Moses to sing the song of praise (&quot;I will&quot; being stronger than &quot;I shall&quot;). 5 tn This causal clause gives the reason for and summary of the praise. The Hebrew expression has כִּי־גָּאֹה גָּאָה (ki ga&apos;oh ga&apos;ah). The basic idea of the verb is &quot;rise up loftily&quot; or &quot;proudly.&quot; But derivatives of the root carry the nuance of majesty or pride (S. R. Driver, Exodus, 132). So the idea of the perfect tense with its infinitive absolute may mean &quot;he is highly exalted&quot; or &quot;he has done majestically&quot; or &quot;he is gloriously glorious.&quot; 6 sn The common understanding is that Egypt did not have people riding horses at this time, and so the phrase the horse and its rider is either viewed as an anachronism or is interpreted to mean charioteers. The word &quot;to ride&quot; can mean on a horse or in a chariot. Some have suggested changing &quot;rider&quot; to &quot;chariot&quot; (re-vocalization) to read &quot;the horse and its chariot.&quot;

7 tn Heb &quot;Yah.&quot; Moses&apos; poem here uses a short form of the name Yahweh, traditionally rendered in English by &quot;the LORD.&quot; 8 tn The word וְזִמְרָת (vÿzimrat) is problematic. It probably had a suffix yod (י) that was accidentally dropped because of the yod (י) on the divine name following. Most scholars posit another meaning for the word. A meaning of &quot;power&quot; fits the line fairly well, forming a hendiadys with strength - &quot;strength and power&quot; becoming &quot;strong power.&quot; Similar lines are in Isa 12:2 and Ps 118:14. Others suggest &quot;protection&quot; or &quot;glory.&quot; However, there is nothing substantially wrong with &quot;my song&quot; in the line - only that it would be a nicer match if it had something to do with strength. 9 tn The word נָוָה (navah) occurs only here. It may mean &quot;beautify, adorn&quot; with praises (see BDB 627 s.v.). See also M. Dahood, &quot;Exodus 15:2: &apos;anwehu and Ugaritic snwt,&quot; Bib 59 (1979): 260-61; and M. Klein, &quot;The Targumic Tosefta to Exodus 15:2,&quot; JJS 26 (1975): 61-67; and S. B. Parker, &quot;Exodus 15:2 Again,&quot; VT 21 (1971): 373-79.

10 tn Heb &quot;man of war&quot; (so KJV, ASV). &quot;Warrior&quot; is now the preferred translation since &quot;man of war&quot; is more commonly known today as a warship. The expression indicates that Yahweh is one who understands how to fight and defeat the enemy. The word &quot;war&quot; modifies &quot;man&quot; to reveal that Yahweh is a warrior. Other passages use similar descriptions: Isa 42:13 has &quot;man of wars&quot;; Ps 24:8 has &quot;mighty man of battle.&quot; See F. Cross, &quot;The Divine Warrior in Israel&apos;s Early Cult,&quot; Biblical Motifs, 11-30. 11 tn Heb &quot;Yahweh is his name.&quot; As throughout, the name &quot;Yahweh&quot; is rendered as &quot;the Lord&quot; in the translation, as is typically done in English translations.

1 sn Exod 16 plays an important part in the development of the book&apos;s theme. It is part of the wider section that is the prologue leading up to the covenant at Sinai, a part of which was the obligation of obedience and loyalty (P. W. Ferris, Jr., &quot;The Manna Narrative of Exodus 16:1-10,&quot; JETS 18 [1975]: 191-99). The record of the wanderings in the wilderness is selective and not exhaustive. It may have been arranged somewhat topically for instructional reasons. U. Cassuto describes this section of the book as a didactic anthology arranged according to association of both context and language (Exodus, 187). Its themes are: lack of vital necessities, murmuring, proving, and providing. All the wilderness stories reiterate the same motifs. So, later, when Israel arrived in Canaan, they would look back and be reminded that it was Yahweh who brought them all the way, in spite of their rebellions. Because he is their Savior and their Provider, he will demand loyalty from them. In the Manna Narrative there is murmuring over the lack of bread (1-3), the disputation with Moses (4-8), the appearance of the glory and the promise of bread (9-12), the provision (13-22), the instructions for the Sabbath (23-30), and the memorial manna (31-36). 2 tn The sentence begins with a preterite and vav (ו) consecutive, which can be subordinated to the next clause with the preterite and vav consecutive. Here it has been treated as a temporal clause. 3 tn The word is often rendered &quot;congregation&quot; (so KJV, ASV, NASB, NRSV), but the modern perception of a congregation is not exactly what is in mind in the desert. Another possible rendering is &quot;community&quot; (NAB, NIV, NCV, TEV) or &quot;assembly.&quot; The Hebrew word is used of both good and bad groups (Judg 14:8; Ps 1:5; 106:17-18). 4 tn The form in the text is לְצֵאתָם (lÿtse&apos;tam, &quot;after their going out&quot;). It clearly refers to their deliverance from Egypt, and so it may be vividly translated.
5 tn Or &quot;community&quot; or &quot;assembly.&quot;

6 tn The text reads: מִי־יִתֵּן מוּתֵנוּ (mi-yitten mutenu, &quot;who will give our dying&quot;) meaning &quot;If only we had died.&quot; מוּתֵנוּ is the Qal infinitive construct with the suffix. This is one way that Hebrew expresses the optative with an infinitive construct. See R. J. Williams, Hebrew Syntax, 91-92, §547. 7 tn The form is a Qal infinitive construct used in a temporal clause, and the verb &quot;when we ate&quot; has the same structure. 8 sn That the complaint leading up to the manna is unjustified can be seen from the record itself. They left Egypt with flocks and herds and very much cattle, and about 45 days later they are complaining that they are without food. Moses reminded them later that they lacked nothing (Deut 3:7; for the whole sermon on this passage, see 8:1-20). Moreover, the complaint is absurd because the food of work gangs was far more meager than they recall. The complaint was really against Moses. They crave the eating of meat and of bread and so God will meet that need; he will send bread from heaven and quail as well. 9 tn לְהָמִית (lÿhamit) is the Hiphil infinitive construct showing purpose. The people do not trust the intentions or the plan of their leaders and charge Moses with bringing everyone out to kill them.

1 sn This is the famous story telling how the people rebelled against Yahweh when they thirsted, saying that Moses had brought them out into the wilderness to kill them by thirst, and how Moses with the staff brought water from the rock. As a result of this the name was called Massa and Meribah because of the testing and the striving. It was a challenge to Moses&apos; leadership as well as a test of Yahweh&apos;s presence. The narrative in its present form serves an important point in the argument of the book. The story turns on the gracious provision of God who can give his people water when there is none available. The narrative is structured to show how the people strove. Thus, the story intertwines God&apos;s free flowing grace with the sad memory of Israel&apos;s sins. The passage can be divided into three parts: the situation and the complaint (1-3), the cry and the miracle (4-6), and the commemoration by naming (7). 2 tn Or &quot;congregation&quot; (KJV, ASV, NASB, NRSV). 3 tn The text says that they journeyed &quot;according to their journeyings.&quot; Since the verb form (and therefore the derived noun) essentially means to pull up the tent pegs and move along, this verse would be saying that they traveled by stages, or, from place to place. 4 sn The location is a bit of a problem. Exod 19:1-2 suggests that it is near Sinai, whereas it is normally located near Kadesh in the north. Without any details provided, M. Noth concludes that two versions came together (Exodus [OTL], 138). S. R. Driver says that the writer wrote not knowing that they were 24 miles apart (Exodus, 157). Critics have long been bothered by this passage because of the two names given at the same place. If two sources had been brought together, it is not possible now to identify them. But Noth insisted that if there were two names there were two different locations. The names Massah and Meribah occur alone in Scripture (Deut 9:22, and Num 20:1 for examples), but together in Ps 95 and in Deut 33:8. But none of these passages is a clarification of the difficulty. Most critics would argue that Massah was a secondary element that was introduced into this account, because Exod 17 focuses on Meribah. From that starting point they can diverge greatly on the interpretation, usually having something to do with a water test. But although Num 20 is parallel in several ways, there are major differences: 1) it takes place 40 years later than this, 2) the name Kadesh is joined to the name Meribah there, and 3) Moses is punished there. One must conclude that if an event could occur twice in similar ways (complaint about water would be a good candidate for such), then there is no reason a similar name could not be given. 5 tn The disjunctive vav introduces a parenthetical clause that is essential for this passage - there was no water. 6 tn Here the construction uses a genitive after the infinitive construct for the subject: &quot;there was no water for the drinking of the people&quot; (GKC 353-54 §115.c).

7 tn The verb וַיָּרֶב (vayyarev) is from the root רִיב (riv); it forms the basis of the name &quot;Meribah.&quot; The word means &quot;strive, quarrel, be in contention&quot; and even &quot;litigation.&quot; A translation &quot;quarrel&quot; does not appear to capture the magnitude of what is being done here. The people have a legal dispute - they are contending with Moses as if bringing a lawsuit. 8 tn The imperfect tense with the vav (ו) follows the imperative, and so it carries the nuance of the logical sequence, showing purpose or result. This may be expressed in English as &quot;give us water so that we may drink,&quot; but more simply with the English infinitive, &quot;give us water to drink.&quot; sn One wonders if the people thought that Moses and Aaron had water and were withholding it from the people, or whether Moses was able to get it on demand. The people should have come to Moses to ask him to pray to God for water, but their action led Moses to say that they had challenged God (B. Jacob, Exodus, 476). 9 tn In this case and in the next clause the imperfect tenses are to be taken as progressive imperfects - the action is in progress. 10 tn The verb נָסָה (nasah) means &quot;to test, tempt, try, prove.&quot; It can be used of people simply trying to do something that they are not sure of (such as David trying on Saul&apos;s armor), or of God testing people to see if they will obey (as in testing Abraham, Gen 22:1), or of people challenging others (as in the Queen of Sheba coming to test Solomon), and of the people in the desert in rebellion putting God to the test. By doubting that God was truly in their midst, and demanding that he demonstrate his presence, they tested him to see if he would act. There are times when &quot;proving&quot; God is correct and required, but that is done by faith (as with Gideon); when it is done out of unbelief, then it is an act of disloyalty.

11 tn The verbs and the pronouns in this verse are in the singular because &quot;the people&quot; is singular in form. 12 tn The demonstrative pronoun is used as the enclitic form for special emphasis in the question; it literally says, &quot;why is this you have brought us up?&quot; (R. J. Williams, Hebrew Syntax, 24, §118). 13 sn Their words deny God the credit for bringing them out of Egypt, impugn the integrity of Moses and God by accusing them of bringing the people out here to die, and show a lack of faith in God&apos;s ability to provide for them.

1 sn This chapter forms the transition to the Law. There has been the deliverance, the testing passages, the provision in the wilderness, and the warfare. Any God who can do all this for his people deserves their allegiance. In chap. 18 the Lawgiver is giving advice, using laws and rulings, but then he is given advice to organize the elders to assist. Thus, when the Law is fully revealed, a system will be in place to administer it. The point of the passage is that a great leader humbly accepts advice from other godly believers to delegate responsibility. He does not try to do it all himself; God does not want one individual to do it all. The chapter has three parts: vv. 1-12 tell how Jethro heard and came and worshiped and blessed; vv. 13-23 have the advice of Jethro, and then vv. 24-27 tell how Moses implemented the plan and Jethro went home. See further E. J. Runions, &quot;Exodus Motifs in 1 Samuel 7 and 8,&quot; EvQ 52 (1980): 130-31; and also see for another idea T. C. Butler, &quot;An Anti-Moses Tradition,&quot; JSOT 12 (1979): 9-15. 2 tn This clause beginning with כִּי (ki) answers the question of what Jethro had heard; it provides a second, explanatory noun clause that is the object of the verb - &quot;he heard (1) all that God had done... (2) that he had brought....&quot; See R. J. Williams, Hebrew Syntax, 81, §490. 3 sn This is an important report that Jethro has heard, for the claim of God that he brought Israel out of bondage in Egypt will be the foundation of the covenant stipulations (Exod 20).
4 tn Heb &quot;he&quot;; the referent (Moses) has been specified in the translation for clarity (also in the following verse).
